headline: mixed
texts: Parts of the primary survey are solid and parts are not yet. The pattern in the sections below shows where you reached for a familiar rule (loudest problem first, usual test first, old key) instead of asking what kills fastest or which qualifier applies. Start with the objectives marked gap or shaky, then the review cards.

Your order was mostly right but not steady. Hold the rule: loss of airway kills faster than loss of breathing, which kills faster than loss of blood volume, so ABCDE follows time to death. Redo the order card once.

You partly have the talking patient. A clear voice means a patent airway for now, so the next step is breathing, not intubation or skipping ahead, and ABCDE is repeated on any deterioration. GCS 8 or less triggers a definitive airway.

The adult and child airway rule is not steady yet. Surgical cricothyroidotomy suits adults; under about 12 years the cricoid is the only complete ring, so needle cricothyroidotomy is used. Check age before choosing.

Tension pneumothorax is partly secure. It is a clinical diagnosis treated with immediate needle decompression then a chest tube, before X-ray or ventilation. Recheck the adult site (4th or 5th space, just in front of the mid-axillary line) against the older 2nd space key.

Your chest contrasts are partly secure. Tension pneumothorax is hyper-resonant with distended neck veins; massive haemothorax is dull with flat veins; tamponade has muffled heart sounds with clear breath sounds. Redo the contrast table.
Shock recognition is partly secure. BP holds until Class III, and children, the elderly and beta-blocked patients can look normal while shocked. Slow pulse with warm skin points to neurogenic shock.
Fluids are partly secure. ATLS 10th edition gives 1 L warmed isotonic crystalloid in adults then early blood, while older keys said 2 L. Permissive hypotension does not apply with a brain injury.
This is partly secure. An unstable patient goes to FAST in the resuscitation room, not CT. With blood at the meatus or a high prostate, a urethrogram precedes the catheter.
You placed the secondary survey correctly: only after the primary survey is complete and resuscitation is under way.
The tranexamic acid detail is shaky. The window is within 3 hours of injury; 8 hours is the length of the second infusion.
The peaks are shaky. First peak is seconds to minutes, second is minutes to hours (the one ATLS targets), third is days to weeks from sepsis.

You first put haemorrhage ahead of airway, then changed. Keep frequency (commonest preventable death) apart from priority (fastest killer). Military MARCH protocols do put bleeding first, but the ATLS exam order is ABCDE. This can return when blood is visible, so reread the order card.

You first treated a talking patient as safe, then corrected. Speech shows a patent airway for now only; it can fail later, as with an expanding neck swelling. Repeat ABCDE with every change, especially under exam pressure.

You first asked for imaging before decompression, then changed. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis; the patient cannot afford the delay. Shock plus the signs is enough, and the habit returns easily.

You first picked CT for an unstable patient or treated FAST as organ-defining, then changed. Unstable goes to FAST or DPL; CT defines injury only in the stable patient. Recheck the ladder before the exam.

You first ventilated or intubated before decompressing, then changed. Positive pressure feeds a one-way valve and raises pressure. Decompress, then secure the airway; the letter order does not override the physiology.

You first called low pressure after trauma haemorrhagic, then changed. A slow pulse with warm dry skin points to neurogenic shock, while haemorrhage gives tachycardia. Hypovolaemia stays the default only until the pulse says otherwise.

You first treated tension pneumothorax and massive haemothorax as one picture, then changed. Both have absent breath sounds, so that finding separates nothing; hyper-resonance with full neck veins is air, dullness with flat veins is blood.

You first gave Beck's triad to tension pneumothorax, then changed. Beck's triad is hypotension, muffled heart sounds and distended neck veins; tamponade has clear breath sounds. Raised neck veins alone are shared.

You first expected low BP early, then changed. Compensation holds systolic pressure until about a third of blood is lost, so hypotension first appears in Class III. Tachycardia and narrow pulse pressure come first.

You first answered the older 2 L key, then changed. ATLS 10th edition says 1 L warmed isotonic crystalloid, then early blood, because large volumes dilute clotting factors and cool the patient. Both keys exist, so read which edition the question follows.

You first gave the older 2nd space mid-clavicular site for an adult, then changed. ATLS 10th edition uses the 4th or 5th space just in front of the mid-axillary line in adults and keeps the 2nd space for children. Be ready for either key.

You first blamed the paradoxical movement for the hypoxia, then changed. The visible sign defines the injury, but the underlying pulmonary contusion causes the hypoxia, so treatment is oxygen, analgesia and cautious fluids.
You first reversed the shift, then changed. Trapped air under pressure pushes the mediastinum and trachea to the opposite side and kinks the great veins; a collapsed lung does not pull them over.

You first trusted normal vital signs in a qualifier patient, then changed. Beta-blockers and age blunt the pulse, children hold pressure until late, and pregnancy hides up to about a third of blood volume. Check the qualifier first.

You first used the adult surgical airway in a child, then changed. Under about 12 years use needle cricothyroidotomy, because the cricoid is the only complete ring and is easily damaged. Check age whenever a surgical airway is on the table.

You first catheterised in a patient with possible urethral injury, then changed. Blood at the meatus or a high-riding prostate means a retrograde urethrogram first. The routine catheter is the habit to watch.
You first linked ATLS to the third peak, then changed. ATLS targets the second peak, minutes to hours after injury, where resuscitation can change the outcome; sepsis and organ failure are the third.
You first applied permissive hypotension in a head-injured patient, then changed. It is not used in traumatic brain injury, where the brain needs adequate perfusion. Check for a head injury first.

You first built the chest list loosely, then changed. The five are tension pneumothorax, open pneumothorax, massive haemothorax, flail chest with contusion, and tamponade assessed under circulation. Simple pneumothorax is not one of them.
You tend to get priorities wrong, choosing by what is visible, common or the first letter. Order by time to death and by physiology, then decide.
You tend to pick the test or step by accuracy or routine, not by stability and warning signs. Ask first whether this patient can afford the delay and whether a sign forbids the routine.

You tend to merge look-alikes: shared findings such as absent breath sounds or low pressure feel like one picture. Before naming a diagnosis, find the one sign that only one condition has (percussion, neck veins, pulse, heart sounds).
You tend to answer with the older exam key. Learn both: what PYQs expected and what ATLS 10th edition says, with the reason for the change.
You tend to reverse direction or cause: sign for cause, collapse for pressure. Predict what happens step by step from the mechanism before choosing.
You tend to drop the qualifier: age, drug, pregnancy or brain injury. Before using a rule, ask who this patient is and whether the rule has an exception.

You tapped Sure on two or more answers that were wrong. Those are the most useful errors, since a confident error corrected is remembered well. Do their review cards first, and before tapping Sure, name the qualifier or discriminating sign that makes you certain.

You asked for hints or explanations often. That is fine while learning, but unaided recall is what the exam tests. Revisit the cards for the objectives where you asked, and answer first before opening help.

Start with the review cards for objectives marked gap, and confident errors first. Do one card per sitting, say the discriminating feature or qualifier aloud, then retest on a fresh question. Revisit the fell-open items after a day.
